content:
Transferring keyboard shortcuts to a programmable macro keyboard is the most effective productivity boost I've ever made.

Stepping into the world of keyboard shortcuts

My first foray into keyboard shortcuts began with simple text triggers in macOS, like using @@ to type out my primary email address, and setting up similar shortcuts for my full name, address, phone number, zip code, and the like.

After that, I decided to take it further and use Keyboard Maestro to set up keyboard shortcuts to open several of my most-used folders and apps.

From Desktop to Downloads, and work-related folders, pressing Fn+F1 through Fn+F6 has become pure muscle memory, taking me instantly to places that would otherwise require a few mouse clicks. Other function keys are dedicated to launching frequently used apps and websites, as well as accessing Keyboard Maestro's clipboard history switcher.

This gradually evolved into automating parts of my workflow, including opening QuickTime and starting a new recording, as well as automatically launching Shure PlusMOTIV whenever I plug in a specific USB-C microphone.

Not long after, I also started customising shortcuts for Adobe Audition's tools, settings, and panels, some of which I quickly moved over to the Logitech MX Master mouse for even faster editing.

Taking it to the next level

This setup served me well for quite some time, until one day my colleague Gui Rambo at 9to5Mac recommended a small macro keyboard with 12 keys and 3 knobs that he had purchased. I was immediately sold and followed suit.

When it arrived, I quickly discovered that getting it to work properly on macOS required some additional setup. Fortunately, this GitHub project handled most of the technical details, and ChatGPT filled in the remaining steps to help me get everything up and running smoothly.

One of the great advantages of this setup is that with a dedicated keyboard for triggering Keyboard Maestro shortcuts, there's no need to memorise key combinations or compromise on ergonomics.

Moreover, since this keyboard can offer up to 3 layers of 12-key shortcuts, and the knobs themselves can also function as buttons, it can operate in one way when I'm using Adobe Audition, and completely transform into another mode when I'm interacting with the system.

When using Adobe Audition, this macro keyboard paired with the MX Master mouse allows me to switch tools, export files (or just specific sections), and apply effects like normalisation, compression, de-reverb, de-essing, and ripple delete with speed and fluidity that's orders of magnitude faster than regular shortcuts—or, God forbid, no shortcuts at all.

When interacting with the system, I can switch the same keyboard to another layer to easily change audio input, adjust volume, tweak display brightness, mute or unmute the microphone, and access frequently used folders.

Admittedly, memorising all these commands took me a little time, but it became second nature faster than you'd think. More importantly, when I need to work away from this setup, the Mac actually feels broken to me.

On top of that, there are countless macro keyboard configurations and options to choose from—different shapes, sizes, keys, knobs, lighting colours, and so on. It's a truly bottomless rabbit hole, and if your work involves any repetitive tasks (and whose doesn't?), I wholeheartedly recommend diving in.
